name: Licorice root extract (glabridin)

lead: Licorice root extract is a botanical ingredient in brightening products, used to lighten dark spots and even out tone. Its main active, glabridin, is promoted for fading pigment.

In cultured mouse melanoma cells, glabridin inhibited tyrosinase, the enzyme that starts melanin synthesis, and in guinea pig skin it affected pigment formation and inflammation. Other licorice compounds such as glabrene and isoliquiritigenin have also been reported as tyrosinase inhibitors, and dermatology reviews list licorice among non-hydroquinone lightening options. No human pigment trial was located for the appearance use.

paras: It appears in serums, creams and brightening products, usually as part of a routine with other lighteners and sunscreen, and is used daily over weeks.
Topical risks are not quantified in the sources reviewed. Large oral licorice intake has documented adverse effects, and some constituents are estrogen-like in lab studies.

angle.text: Licorice extract is used in brightening products to lighten dark spots and even tone, with glabridin blocking tyrosinase so less melanin is produced. This has been shown in cell studies; no human pigment trials were located for the appearance use.

lead: Licorice root extract, from Glycyrrhiza glabra, is a botanical ingredient used in cosmetic brightening products to even out skin tone. Its main skin-active component is glabridin, a hydrophobic isoflavane found in the root extract and listed in the International Nomenclature of Cosmetic Ingredients.[1][2][3]

People use it in serums and creams aimed at an even, brighter-looking complexion, with the aim of fading the look of dark spots and post-inflammatory marks. The chain is laboratory-based: glabridin inhibited tyrosinase, the key enzyme of melanin production, in cultured mouse melanoma cells, and had inhibitory effects on melanogenesis and inflammation in guinea pig skin; other licorice constituents such as glabrene and isoliquiritigenin were also reported as tyrosinase inhibitors.[4][5]

A 2020 dermatology review lists licorice root extract among the top 10 cosmeceuticals for facial hyperpigmentation, alongside thiamidol, kojic acid, vitamin C, arbutin, retinol, nicotinamide, ferulic acid, resorcinol and soy, and a 2007 review places licorice-derived agents among non-hydroquinone lightening options.[6][7] Human trials of licorice or glabridin specifically for facial pigmentation have not been published; registered trials of licorice extracts concern other conditions.
infobox: Root of Glycyrrhiza glabra (liquorice), a perennial legume [3]
Insoluble in water; soluble in organic solvents such as propylene glycol [2]

paras: Glycyrrhiza glabra is a herbaceous perennial legume in the bean family, native to West Asia, North Africa and southern Europe, with roots that are harvested in autumn two to three years after planting. The name derives from the Greek glykyrrhiza, meaning sweet root. [3] Carl Linnaeus described the species in 1753. [3]

The root's best-known constituent is glycyrrhizin, a sweet glycoside that makes up roughly 7 to 10 percent of the root depending on cultivation; the root also contains triterpenoids, polyphenols and polysaccharides, and its flavonoids give it a yellow colour. [3] Glabridin and glabrene are classed as phytoestrogens. [3] Cosmetic brightening interest centres on the oil-soluble flavonoid fraction rather than on glycyrrhizin, the compound associated with the sweetness and with the oral safety concerns. [4][3]

In cosmetics, licorice extract is formulated as a botanical alternative to hydroquinone and other lighteners for dark spots, melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.[6][7] The 2020 review of cosmeceuticals frames most of these ingredients as working through tyrosinase inhibition, used alone or alongside established treatments.[7] Licorice is also used beyond skin: reviews cover dental, cardiovascular and other traditional uses.[8][9][10]

sections.h: Appearance uses and how it is meant to work
paras: For appearance, licorice root extract is used to even out skin tone. Dark spots, melasma and post-inflammatory marks left by acne make skin look uneven, and licorice extract is sold as a botanical brightening ingredient intended to fade them. The chain is: glabridin, the main skin-relevant compound of the oil-soluble fraction of the extract, inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme that drives melanin production; less melanin production means paler marks over time and a more uniform complexion.[4][7]

The 2020 dermatologic review of the top ten cosmeceuticals for facial hyperpigmentation lists licorice root extract alongside thiamidol, kojic acid, vitamin C, arbutin, retinol, nicotinamide, ferulic acid, resorcinol and soy, describes the group as a possibly safer alternative that can be used alone or alongside established treatments, and notes that many of them are thought to act through tyrosinase inhibition.[7] A second angle is calming: licorice compounds have anti-inflammatory activity in laboratory work, which proponents connect to reducing the redness and irritation that precede post-inflammatory pigment.[1][11]

Glabridin is a yellowish-brown powder of formula C20H20O4, classed as an isoflavane and natural phenol, and appears in the International Nomenclature of Cosmetic Ingredients.[2] A 1998 study described it as the main component of the hydrophobic fraction of licorice extract relevant to skin.[4]

Licorice was among the most widely prescribed herbs in ancient Egyptian, Roman, Greek and East Asian medicine, according to a review of its ethnopharmacology.[8] The skin-lightening interest dates in the sources to a 1998 laboratory study of glabridin in Pigment Cell Research, followed by a 2003 report on glabrene and isoliquiritigenin.[4][5]

A 2007 dermatology review placed skin-lightening preparations in a long clinical context: they are used by people of all Fitzpatrick skin types, with types I to III needing local lightening for hormonally induced melasma and post-inflammatory pigment from acne and trauma, and darker skin types having an even greater need for lightening for social reasons and for pigment changes around the eyes, in skin folds and after dermatitis.[6] That review's title refers to the hydroquinone controversy, the debate over the safety of the standard lightening agent, which is the background against which botanical ingredients like licorice gained attention.[6]

The structure of glabridin was reported in 1996 by Kinoshita and colleagues in a paper on isoflavan derivatives from G. glabra. [2] Licorice itself has a long record in traditional medicine; in Chinese medicine the related species G. uralensis is believed to harmonize formulas. [3]

In the 1998 laboratory study, glabridin inhibited tyrosinase in B16 murine melanoma cells at concentrations of roughly 0.1 to 1.0 microgram per milliliter without a detectable effect on their DNA synthesis, and a licorice fraction showed effects on melanogenesis and inflammation in guinea pig skin.[4] A 2003 paper reported glabrene and isoliquiritigenin as additional tyrosinase inhibitors from licorice roots.[5]
Licorice compounds have also been studied for anti-inflammatory activity, which is sometimes cited as relevant to post-inflammatory pigment.[11][12]

A review of licorice describes broad anti-inflammatory activity, and glabridin has also been studied for antioxidant effects on LDL and, in cells, against dexamethasone-induced muscle atrophy.[1][12][13]

No studies found of licorice root extract or glabridin for skin lightening in people. A randomized trial examined the clinical safety of a licorice flavonoid oil and the pharmacokinetics of glabridin in healthy humans, and small trials examined glabridin and LDL oxidation.[14] Registered clinical trials of licorice extracts examine other conditions, such as hypertension, caries prevention, diabetic neuropathy, menopausal symptoms and stroke.[15][16][17] Evidence for the pigment use is therefore limited to laboratory and animal work.

The 2007 randomised study of licorice flavonoid oil in healthy humans assessed clinical safety and the pharmacokinetics of glabridin after oral intake, which tells researchers how the compound is absorbed but is not a test of skin colour.[14] Two small randomised trials, published in 2009 and 2008, examined glabridin's effect on oxidation of LDL cholesterol, a cardiovascular outcome.[18][19] Registered trials include licorice for home blood pressure (NCT05661721), for dental caries (NCT03763578) and for postmenopausal symptoms (NCT01170195), none of which concern pigment.[15][16][17]
Glabridin has also been examined for platelet inhibition; a 2022 study reported that effect in humans and mice, which concerns cardiovascular research rather than pigment. [2]

Licorice taken by mouth in large amounts has been associated with documented adverse effects; a 2012 review of licorice abuse describes the problem as significant enough to warrant a warning message.[20] Some licorice constituents, including glabrene and isoliquiritigenin, show estrogen-like activity in laboratory studies.[21][22] These findings concern oral or experimental exposure; the risks of topical cosmetic use have not been quantified.

A review of licorice's effects on the cardiovascular system and the 2012 review of licorice abuse cover systemic effects reported with large oral intakes of licorice, and the published safety literature on topical licorice extract for the skin is limited.[20][10]

Reviews of liquorice describe corticosteroid-like effects from heavy oral intake, including hypertension, low potassium, oedema and muscle weakness, and advise avoiding it during pregnancy. [3] Regulatory bodies consider licorice-containing foods generally recognized as safe if not consumed excessively, and some jurisdictions suggest limits on daily glycyrrhizin intake. [3] These oral thresholds relate to glycyrrhizin, not to the glabridin-rich extracts used topically. [3]

Licorice extract is marketed as a botanical alternative within the wider market of non-hydroquinone lighteners, a category discussed in dermatology reviews against the background of debate over hydroquinone.[6]

Wikipedia notes that glabridin is listed in the International Nomenclature of Cosmetic Ingredients, which means it appears under its own name on product labels, and it is described there as insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents such as propylene glycol, a property that shapes which formulas can carry it.[2] Licorice root extract is one ingredient in the wider family of non-hydroquinone brighteners, which dermatology reviews discuss together with arbutin, kojic acid, vitamin C and others.[6][7]

Because glabridin is hydrophobic, formulations use oil-phase or solvent-based carriers, and products typically list it alongside other brighteners. [2][7] Dermatology reviews describe the cosmeceutical category as a potentially safer alternative to prescription lighteners that can be used alone or combined with established treatments. [7]
